slides.title: ETCO2 climbing. Jaw rigid. HR racing.
slides.sub: Malignant hyperthermia: your first five minutes.

slides.pearl: Fever is often a LATE sign. Don't wait for it.

slides.body: Turn off the volatile agent. Get the MH cart and extra hands. Tell the surgeon to stop or finish fast.
100% O2 at high fresh gas flow. Add activated charcoal filters if you have them. Don't waste time changing machines.
Assign people to mix it immediately. Repeat per MHAUS guidance until signs resolve.

slides.title: MH Hotline: 1-800-644-9737
slides.body: MHAUS, 24/7. Save this before your next case.

caption:
ETCO2 keeps climbing even as you turn up the ventilation. Would you think MH first? 🔥

Swipe for the first five minutes: stop triggers and call for help → hyperventilate with 100% O2 at high flow → dantrolene immediately → cool, treat K+ and arrhythmias, send labs.

💡 Hyperthermia is often late. Rising ETCO2 and tachycardia come first.

scene: PACU. Drowsy after an opioid-heavy case. Snoring, then quiet.
question: First move?
why: Stimulate, open the airway, give oxygen, and check ventilation. Then find the cause: opioid, residual block, or sedation. Naloxone if opioid hypoventilation persists.
pearl: Support the airway first. Then chase the cause.
caption:
PACU, SpO2 88%, RR 7, patient drowsy after an opioid-heavy case. What's your very first move? 😴

Comment your pick before the answer 👇

Open the airway and oxygenate first, then work out why: opioids, residual neuromuscular block, or lingering sedation. Treat the cause once the patient is safe.

scene: Beach-chair shoulder, interscalene block. Sudden crash 50 min in.
question: What's happening?
why: Upright position pools blood. An underfilled, vigorously contracting ventricle triggers a vagal reflex: sudden bradycardia and hypotension. Lower the head, give fluid, treat rate and pressure fast.
pearl: In the beach chair, the brain sits above your BP cuff.
caption:
Beach-chair shoulder under an interscalene block. BP 72/38, HR 42, out of nowhere. What's happening? 🪑

The Bezold-Jarisch reflex: an underfilled, hyperdynamic ventricle triggers a vagal response. Lower the head, give volume, and treat the bradycardia and hypotension quickly.

💡 The brain sits above the cuff, so cerebral perfusion is lower than the number you see.

📌 Save this for your regional rotation.

scene: Labor epidural, one-sided all night. Urgent C-section called.
question: Best plan?
why: A patchy labor epidural often fails as a surgical block. If time allows, replace it. If not, prepare for GA with an airway plan. A spinal after a large top-up risks a high block.
pearl: Speak up early: a bad labor epidural is a C-section problem waiting to happen.
caption:
One-sided labor epidural all night, and now an urgent C-section is called. Do you trust it? 🤰

Comment your pick before the answer 👇

A patchy labor epidural often won't become a reliable surgical block. Replace it early when you can; when you can't, have the GA and airway plan ready. A full spinal after a large epidural top-up can spread high.

scene: Spinal for C-section. Three minutes after placement.
question: Which pressor?
why: Phenylephrine is first-line for spinal hypotension, but its reflex slowing would push HR 54 even lower. With bradycardia, ephedrine supports both pressure and rate. Treat fast: uterine blood flow follows maternal BP.
pearl: Phenylephrine is first-line. Bradycardia changes the choice.
caption:
Spinal for C-section. BP 78/40, HR 54. Phenylephrine or ephedrine? 💉

Comment your pick before the answer 👇

Phenylephrine is first-line for spinal hypotension in obstetrics, but reflex bradycardia matters when HR is already low. With hypotension plus bradycardia, ephedrine supports both pressure and rate.
